RealSI is a benchmark for Simultaneous Interpretation(SI) in real-world scenarios.
Audio data are collected from public videos, covering 2 languages and 10 different topics.
We cut out video clips of 3-7 minutes, and label the timestamps, transcripts and translations of speech in the video.
The utterances are grouped in semantic segments, which convey complete semantic for translation.
When conducting human evaluation, we recommend evaluating the model prediction results according to this segmentation.
This dataset is released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.
We do not own the copyright of the videos and only release our annotation together with the publicly available website links of the corresponding videos.

First, these benchmarks often contain speeches that are either recorded by volunteers (e.g. CoVoST and FLUERS) or collected from formally, clearly, and fluently talk and podcasts by well-prepared speakers (e.g. MuST-C and GigaST).
Consequently, evaluations on manually segmented datasets are likely to overestimate the performances of a real-world SiST system.
RealSI is collected from diverse sources, and most speakers talk naturally and casually without careful preparation.
We choose 10 popular domains: technology, healthcare, education, finance, law, environment, entertainment, science, sports, and art.
Each sample in RealSI is a nearly 5-minute speech to mock SiST without manual segmentation.
For systems that cannot take long-form audio as input, we also provide sentence-level timestamps for segmentation.
Table 2: Statistics of our proposed RealSI benchmark.
Table 2 presents the detailed statistics of our RealSI.

Due to the limitations in human evaluation capacity, the VIP scores are calculated on 4 randomly selected samples out of 10 in RealSI across all systems for fair comparison, while automatic metrics are evaluated on 10 samples.
In document level evaluations, each translation of a nearly 5-minute audio was considered one instance.
Note that we only consider a system is better than others when the VIP is higher.
The percentage of valid information fragments within a complete speech session is defined as VIP, which is consistent with real-world criteria for human simultaneous interpretation
We define the key indicator as the “Valid Information Proportion,” denoted as VIP.
A semantic fragment is deemed valid if it effectively conveys the core information, accurately representing the speaker’s original intent.
In this paper, we adopt the widely-used Average Lagging (AL) [45], Length Adaptive Average Lagging (LAAL) [52] for comparing the latency of different methods.
We also propose an additional metric, First Letter Appearance Lagging (FLAL), to reflect user experience on each system.
FLAL represents the time that each system outputs the first determined translation.
We find that the existing metrics AL and LAAL are not suitable latency measurements of paragraph-level SiST on RealSI.
The typical EVS of professional human interpreters usually ranges from 3 to 6 seconds [26] to achieve high-quality translation.
To the publication date of this paper, we collected 14 user surveys on zh-en direction, each user using CLASI for at least 30 minutes.
Although we achieved significant improvements over commercial systems in Chinese-to-English and English-to-Chinese tasks, more languages should be considered in the future.
Furthermore, we argue that the current automatic metrics are not comprehensive for SiST evaluation.
Most of the quality measurements do not consider key information, which is crucial in SiST scenarios.

In the real-world scenarios, where the speeches are often disfluent, informal, and unclear, CLASI achieves VIP of 81.3% and 78.0% for Chinese-to-English and English-to-Chinese translation directions, respectively.
In contrast, state-of-the-art commercial or open-source systems only achieve 35.4% and 41.6%.
Note that the term here is defined as special keywords, such as name, location, abbreviation, and domain-specific word.
We compared Hy-SimulMT with several open-source simultaneous translation models and commercial APIs on the open-source RealSI long-form audio benchmark.
The results show that Hy-SimulMT achieves competitive translation quality at lower latency.
Its GEMBA score exceeded those of the compared open-source models and four of the five commercial APIs.
Hy-SimulMT achieved a StreamLAAL of approximately 3 seconds , the lowest among the systems shown in the comparison.

The horizontal axis shows StreamLAAL, a measure of streaming translation lag, in seconds (lower is better); the vertical axis shows the GEMBA translation quality score (higher is better). StreamLAAL is not the same as the time to first speech output.

In addition to long-form audio, we evaluated the model on four public short-form audio benchmarks—FLEURS, CoVoST2, ACL6060, and RealSI-Sentence—to examine translation performance under different data conditions.
Hy-SimulMT scored higher than the other open-source models in the table on FLEURS, ACL6060, and RealSI-Sentence.
Its 84.7 on RealSI-Sentence was the highest among all listed systems.
Higher scores are better.
These findings apply only to the samples, participating interpreters, and evaluation settings used in this test.
They do not constitute a comprehensive assessment of speech quality, voice similarity, or other dimensions.
